description: As a solo competitor, I'm taking on "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!" I'm particularly interested in analyzing environmental time series, identifying trends and seasonality, applying statistical methods, and turning scientific data into meaningful insights.
summary: Trend Court helps students and curious members of the public answer a simple question: "Is this really changing where I live, or does it just feel that way?" details:
Trend Court helps students and curious members of the public answer a simple question: "Is this really changing where I live, or does it just feel that way?" The user picks a worry (heat, rain and drought, or soil water) and a region. Trend Court then puts that trend "on trial" and returns a verdict backed by evidence, not just a plot.


Two engines do the work:

  • The Clerk gathers the evidence. It loads 45 years (1981–2025) of monthly NASA POWER data and averages 9 sample points across the region, using latitude weights. It refuses records shorter than 20 years or with more than 10% of months missing. It removes the seasonal cycle, and it records the source, the request URLs and the access date for every number.
  • The Examiner tests the evidence. It estimates the rate of change per decade with a Theil–Sen slope and a 95% confidence interval. It tests significance with a Mann–Kendall test that uses the Hamed–Rao correction for autocorrelation. It also runs a seasonal Mann–Kendall test as a consistency check.

The case is then cross-examined. Does the trend hold up if you move the start and end years (window sensitivity)? Does an independent dataset agree (a "witness"), such as NOAA GHCN-CAMS for temperature, GPCP V3.2 for precipitation, or FLDAS for soil moisture? The verdict is one of five labels: Strong evidence, Moderate evidence, Inconclusive, Witnesses disagree, or No detectable trend. Every label is shown next to the numbers behind it.

For example, the Mexicali Valley temperature case finds warming of about +0.39 °C per decade since 1981. The autocorrelation-corrected Mann–Kendall test gives p < 0.001, and the seasonal test agrees.
dataRefs: NASA GES DISC (Goddard Earth Sciences Data and Information Services Center)
projectRefs: NOAA PSL GPCP Version 2.3 Combined Precipitation Data Set
